practical_skills: Choosing between saving and debt payoff

sections.skill: Size, build, and use an emergency fund

questions.prompt: What is an emergency fund for?

choices.text: Planned purchases such as a vacation next summer
Investing in stocks for the highest return
Unexpected costs such as a car repair or a job loss
Paying for holiday gifts each December

questions.correct_answer: Unexpected costs such as a car repair or a job loss
questions.intro: An emergency fund is money saved for unexpected events: a lost job, a medical bill, a car repair. It helps you avoid high-cost borrowing when surprises happen. A common guideline is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses, built up gradually. Even a small fund helps.
questions.feedback: Emergency funds cover unplanned needs; planned goals and investing belong elsewhere.

misconceptions.D: Predictable expense; belongs in a sinking fund

questions.prompt: Where is the best place to keep an emergency fund?

choices.text: An insured savings account she can reach quickly
A stock fund, because it grows faster on average
A 5-year CD with a large early-withdrawal penalty
Cash in a drawer at home

questions.correct_answer: An insured savings account she can reach quickly
questions.intro: Emergency money must be safe and available quickly. Insured savings accounts keep the money stable and accessible. Investments can lose value right when you need them, and long-term CDs charge penalties for early withdrawal.
questions.feedback: Safety and quick access matter most for emergency money.

misconceptions.D: Risk of theft or loss; no interest

sections.relationship: Knowing which costs are surprises explains why an emergency fund is separate from goal savings.

questions.prompt: Which expense is UNEXPECTED?

choices.text: A dentist visit for a cracked tooth
Monthly rent
A yearly car registration
A phone bill

questions.correct_answer: A dentist visit for a cracked tooth
questions.intro: Expected expenses are known in advance (rent, bills, registration). Unexpected expenses are surprises (repairs, medical costs, job loss).
questions.feedback: A cracked tooth is a surprise expense.

questions.feedback: Emergency funds handle surprises; sinking funds handle known costs.

questions.prompt: Kyle has $1,000 saved and a $2,000 credit card balance at 24% APR. Many planners suggest which approach?

choices.text: Keep a small starter fund while paying down the card aggressively
Spend the $1,000 on wants, then pay minimums
Never pay the card until the fund reaches six months
Close the savings account and stop saving

questions.correct_answer: Keep a small starter fund while paying down the card aggressively
questions.intro: High-interest debt grows quickly, but with no savings at all, the next surprise goes back on the card. A common approach: keep a small starter emergency fund, then put extra money toward high-interest debt, then build the full fund.
questions.feedback: A starter fund prevents new debt while extra payments shrink costly debt.

questions.prompt: Why might someone still keep a few hundred dollars in savings while paying debt?

choices.text: Because savings accounts require it by law
Because card interest stops when you have savings
Because debt does not cost anything
So a small surprise does not go back on the card

questions.correct_answer: So a small surprise does not go back on the card
questions.feedback: A small cushion breaks the cycle of new debt.

Send the former card payments to build the full emergency fund

questions.feedback: Redirecting the payment amount builds savings quickly.
